issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessing domestic violence, the trigger pattern is strongly male-linked ('being alone with men') but also includes 'being alone with women' without any corresponding formulation or symptom content explaining why both genders would be equivalently triggering. That broadens the trigger profile in a way that is hard to connect to the rest of the report, which is centered on interpersonal threat from others who might harm him rather than gender-nonspecific social presence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Driving/being a passenger in a vehicle' is difficult to link to the reported trauma and the rest of the profile. No other trigger, threat, or memory item involves transport, accidents, escape, or vehicles, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain not represented elsewhere in the five components.

vignette:
Noah was 18 when he first came to treatment, living in the United States and working as a project manager while trying to keep pace with an adult life that still felt newly assembled. He had grown up in an Oceania family, and he spoke about himself as someone who had learned early to stay alert and not take safety for granted. The traumatic memories that brought him to therapy dated back to childhood, to nights when he witnessed domestic violence in the home. He did not describe one single scene in a smooth sequence; instead, when he tried to talk about it, the account came in disconnected pieces. He remembered flashes of raised voices, the sense of being small and unable to stop what was happening, and then abrupt gaps where whole parts of the event seemed missing. He would stop mid-sentence and say that it felt as though he was only remembering parts of what happened, with the rest gone or out of reach. What remained carried the same terror he had felt then, so that even years later recalling it could pull him back into the body-level fear of being a child in the middle of something frightening and uncontrollable.

Over time, certain situations took on a particular force because they resembled elements of those childhood experiences. Being alone with men was one of the clearest triggers for Noah. He could sit with a male coworker in a meeting without anything happening, yet if he found himself alone in a room or hallway with a man, his attention narrowed sharply and he became intensely aware of exit routes, tone of voice, and body position. He described watching other people closely for signs that they might harm him, studying faces and movements as if he needed to identify danger before it had a chance to unfold. At work, this meant that even ordinary interactions could become exhausting. As a project manager, he was expected to coordinate with colleagues and move through shared spaces with ease, but he often arranged himself so that he would not be isolated with men longer than necessary. He also found himself avoiding other people more generally, keeping conversations brief and limiting contact outside what he considered essential. The pattern had spread into his daily life, shrinking how much he felt able to participate in work and relationships, even as he remained outwardly functional.

Another powerful trigger was his bicycle. Noah explained that the bike itself was not frightening in abstraction; what got to him was the way it could carry him into situations that felt exposed and hard to control. Seeing a bicycle, using one, or even being near them could bring back an uneasy bodily memory of vulnerability and sudden alertness. He did not speak of it as a symbolic trigger, but as something that immediately put him on edge, like his body had already decided it was unsafe before he had time to think. The smell of alcohol worked in a similarly immediate way. If he caught alcohol on someone’s breath or noticed it in a room, he became tense and watchful, as though a familiar danger had entered the space. He had come to avoid people, and his substance use sat alongside that avoidance: he said he smoked, and he drank alcohol and sometimes used medication or drugs, describing these as things he turned to in the course of trying to get through the day rather than as a solution to anything.

In the months before he sought help, Noah’s home life had become organized around checking. He repeatedly checked that doors and windows were locked, sometimes returning to the same lock several times before he could settle. Ordinary sounds also set him off; he jumped or startled at noises that would not bother most people, and this left him feeling embarrassed as well as tense. He would scan rooms, listen for movement in the house, and wake himself up with the need to be certain everything was secure. These habits wore on him and on his relationship, because the people around him could see that he was on guard even when nothing obvious was happening. Still, he experienced these behaviors as necessary precautions. He was not convinced that danger was present every moment, but he was equally unconvinced that it was absent.

What brought Noah in now was that the pattern had become harder to hide and harder to live with. He was tired of feeling cut off from other people, tired of the repeated checking, and tired of being pulled back into the same fear whenever a trigger appeared. He wanted help making sense of why the memories still felt broken and why they still arrived with such terror, and he hoped to feel less trapped by the vigilance that had come to shape his days. At the same time, he was most afraid that if he let his guard down, something he could not control would happen again.
